title: After-school tutoring: live tutor vs. AI homework apps (and when your kid needs which)
summary: Compare live after-school tutoring with AI homework apps like Photomath and Khanmigo. Learn when each works best and how to combine both for your kid.
body_markdown:
Your kid gets home at 3:30pm with a math worksheet they don't understand. You have two options that didn't exist five years ago: open an AI homework app on their phone, or log in to a 30-minute session with a live tutor. Both promise to help. They do very different things.


AI homework tools like Photomath, Khanmigo, and Brainly have gotten remarkably good at walking kids through problem sets. They're instant, they're affordable (often free), and they never lose patience. But they also can't tell if your kid is guessing, nodding along without understanding, or quietly building a habit of outsourcing their thinking.


This comparison breaks down when each approach works best, what to watch for with both, and how to decide which fits your kid's after-school routine.


## What AI homework apps do well


AI tutoring apps have a genuine place in a kid's learning toolkit. Here's where they shine:


**Immediate answers to procedural questions.** If your kid knows *how* to do long division but forgot a step, Photomath can show them the process in 30 seconds. No scheduling, no cost, no waiting.


**Repetitive practice with feedback.** Khanmigo (built on Khan Academy's exercise library) and IXL generate unlimited practice problems and adjust difficulty based on performance. For a kid who needs 50 reps to lock in multiplication facts, this is efficient.


**Low-pressure environment.** Some kids freeze up when a human is watching them work. An app doesn't judge, doesn't sigh, and doesn't move on before they're ready. For kids with[math anxiety](https://outschool.com/study-tips/math-anxiety-in-kids) , this can be a real advantage.


**Always available.** Sunday night at 9pm, your kid realizes they have a science worksheet due Monday. No live tutor is available. An AI app is.


### Watch for


- **Answer-giving disguised as teaching.** Photomath shows steps, but a kid can screenshot a problem and copy the answer without understanding any of them. The app can't tell the difference between learning and copying.
- **No accountability.** Nobody checks in next week to ask, "Did that concept click?" AI apps are transactional. They solve the problem in front of them and move on.
- **Conceptual limits.** AI handles procedural math well (solve this equation, factor this expression) but struggles with "why" questions. If your kid doesn't understand *why* you multiply before you add, an app will keep showing them *how* without addressing the gap.
- **ESA eligibility.** Most free AI apps are not ESA-eligible expenses. If you're using[Education Savings Account funds](https://outschool.com/esa-guides/what-is-education-savings-account) , a subscription app may not qualify, but live tutoring with a certified teacher typically does. Check your state's[approved expenses list](https://outschool.com/esa-guides/approved-list) .


## What live after-school tutoring does well


A live tutor, whether 1:1 or in a small group, brings something an algorithm can't replicate: the ability to read your kid.


**Diagnosing the real problem.** Your kid says they "don't get fractions." A tutor spends 10 minutes and figures out that your kid actually understands fractions fine but is confused by the word-problem format. That distinction changes the entire approach.


**Teaching metacognition.** Good tutors don't just teach math. They teach kids how to approach a problem they've never seen before: "What do you know? What are you looking for? What's the first thing you'd try?" These thinking skills transfer across subjects and don't develop from an app that hands you the next step.


**Accountability across sessions.** A tutor who sees your kid weekly notices patterns. They see that your kid aces computation but falls apart on story problems, or that they understand the concept in the session but can't apply it independently by Wednesday. That longitudinal view is where real progress happens.


**Social learning (small groups).** In a small-group tutoring session with 3-5 kids working on the same topic, kids hear how their peers think through problems. A kid who has been stuck on a concept for a week might hear another kid explain it in a way that clicks instantly. For subjects like[Algebra 1, where math anxiety peaks](https://outschool.com/study-tips/math-anxiety-in-kids) , learning alongside peers who are also struggling normalizes the challenge.


### Watch for


- **Passive sessions.** If a tutor spends 30 minutes solving problems while your kid watches, that's an expensive version of a YouTube video. Good tutoring means the kid does most of the work.
- **Mismatched expertise.** A general "homework help" tutor may not have the subject-depth your kid needs. Ask about the tutor's background in the specific subject.
- **Schedule rigidity.** Some tutoring platforms require a standing weekly appointment. That works for some families, but if your kid only needs help the week before a test, look for on-demand or drop-in options.
